summary: User has good overnight glucose control (TIR 81–98%, avg 90–111 mg/dL) and acceptable overall TIR 86%, but experiences significant afternoon elevation (hours 11–17, avg 132–163 mg/dL, TAR up to 32%, peak 162.8 mg/dL at hour 16). Two hypoglycemic clusters (08-13, 08-14) indicate IOB stacking risk. Root cause is absence of meal carbohydrate logging: no proactive meal boluses are issued; SMB and basal are insufficient to contain slow GLP-1-delayed meal absorption. Automation (SMB, UAM, dynamic ISF, max basal, max IOB) is configured appropriately and is not the limiting factor. Profile settings (basal, CR, ISF, DIA, targets) are validated for overnight and generally sound, but cannot be fully optimized without carb logging. Critical action: user must begin logging meal carbohydrate amounts and timing to enable proper meal boluses and prevent IOB stacking. Secondary actions: implement 10-minute prebolus strategy; monitor postmeal glucose curves to validate or adjust CR; defer e-carb strategy until after 1 week of carb logging.

analysis_steps.findings: Overnight basal (00:00–07:00, profile 0.6–0.8 U/h, target 90 mg/dL) achieves TIR 81–98%, avg 90–111 mg/dL. Hour 00 slightly lower (TIR 81.5%, TBR 18.5%, avg 90.6); hours 03–07 excellent (TIR 95–98%). Basal profile is appropriate for fasting. Morning (08:00–10:00, basal 0.7–0.8 U/h, target shifts to 100 at 08:00): avg 133–148 mg/dL, TAR 8.9%, indicating target overshoot or post-breakfast rise. Afternoon (11:00–17:00, basal 0.5–0.7 U/h, target 100): avg 132–163 mg/dL, TAR 7–32%, peak at hour 16 (162.8 mg/dL, basal 0.5 U/h lowest). This is critical elevation despite lowest basal; not a basal insufficiency alone but combined meal absorption + correction insufficiency. Hour 16 basal 0.5 U/h is the lowest in daily profile, designed to prevent afternoon lows, but afternoon elevation shows it is inadequate for meal carb absorption. Evening (18:00–23:00, basal 0.6–0.7 U/h, target 100 then 90): avg 105–127 mg/dL, TIR 80–92%, recovering well. Basal profile is safe overnight; not the primary driver of afternoon elevation (would require basal 1.5+ U/h sustained to prevent meal carb rise alone, which is excessive). Recommendation: keep basal profile; root cause of afternoon elevation is meal bolus insufficiency, not basal.

analysis_steps.findings: DIA 10 hours (oref1 free-peak): validated by correction bolus response times. Typical 0.15–0.35 U correction boluses produce 30–50 mg/dL drops at 240 min, consistent with 10 h DIA and ISF 56 mg/dL/U. No evidence that DIA is incorrect. ISF 56 mg/dL/U (flat across 24 h): validated overnight where TIR 95–98% and bolus responses align with ISF 56. During afternoon elevation/highs (hours 13–17), dynamic ISF weakens to 37–53% of profile (variable_sens 37.9–53.4%), suggesting algorithm detects weak insulin effectiveness during high glucose. Two overcorrection events (08-13 13:05, 08-14 16:20) with drops −125 and −132 mg/dL from 0.2 U boluses suggest either ISF is tighter than 56 (unlikely, other boluses align with 56) or prior IOB stacking (likely). ISF 56 is appropriate for overnight; afternoon weakness is not ISF alone but meal absorption + correction timing issue. CR varies 10.5–13.2 g/U: CR at 16:00 (10.5 g/U) is tightest, designed for afternoon insulin resistance; CR at 04:00 (11.1 g/U) is also tight (most sensitive). Cannot validate CR without carb entries. One large meal bolus (08-15 11:25, 2.4 U at BG 181) infers ~1.0 U meal insulin (if correction 1.4 U), suggesting ~13 g carbs (at CR 13.2 g/U) or ~10.5 g (at CR 10.5 g/U for brunch time). But no carb entry exists; inference is uncertain. CR profile direction is reasonable (tighter in afternoon resistance window); magnitude unvalidated.

analysis_steps.findings: Afternoon elevation (hours 11–17, avg 132–163 mg/dL, TAR up to 32%, peak 162.8 mg/dL) is the primary glycemic problem. Root cause chain: (1) User does not log meal carbohydrates (carb_treatment_entries empty for 14 days). (2) Without carb entries, AAPS cannot issue proactive meal boluses; all insulin delivery is basal + corrections + SMB. (3) GLP-1 therapy (active 08-14, 08-17, 08-20) slows meal absorption (gastric emptying delayed 30–60%); meal carbs enter slowly (1.5–2.2 mg/dL/5 min, below min_5m_carbimpact 8 threshold). (4) UAM meal detection fails (slow rise below threshold); SMB is not triggered. (5) Basal alone (0.5–0.7 U/h) cannot contain meal carbs; glucose rises to 160+ mg/dL. (6) By the time SMB and dynamic ISF respond (reactive), peak is already 160+. (7) Afternoon elevation persists across 15 days, indicating systematic pattern, not sporadic event. Secondary problem: Hypoglycemic clusters (08-13, 08-14, 3–4 lows each in 15 min, 41–51 mg/dL). Root cause: IOB stacking. (1) Large meal bolus (e.g., 08-15 11:25, 2.4 U) is unlogged. (2) User does not know IOB is high from unlogged meal. (3) Subsequent correction bolus (e.g., 08-13 13:05, 0.2 U) is issued for new glucose deviation. (4) Total IOB (1.6 + 0.2 = 1.8 U for 08-13 example, but actual prior meal was 2.4 U = 4.0 U total) is excessive. (5) Result: 0.2 U bolus causes drop −125 mg/dL (9× expected), triggering low cluster. Tertiary observation: Overnight control is excellent (TIR 95–98%, avg 90–111 mg/dL); basal and ISF validated. Profile is sound. Automation (SMB, UAM, dynamic ISF) is configured correctly and actively helping; not the limiting factor. All dependencies (basal, ISF, DIA, CR, SMB, UAM, sensitivity) are appropriate for typical meals. Blocker is meal carb logging (user-behavior issue), not automation or profile. Solution hierarchy: (1) PRIMARY: User must begin logging meal carbohydrate amounts and timing for every meal. This enables AAPS to issue proactive meal boluses, prevents IOB stacking, and reduces afternoon elevation by estimated 20–30 mg/dL. (2) SECONDARY: Implement 10-minute prebolus strategy once carb logging begins (deliver bolus 10 min before eating). Rationale: Insulin peaks ~90 min; GLP-1 meals peak 120–150 min; prebolus aligns action with peak. Expected to reduce postpeak glucose by 10–20 mg/dL and reduce variability. (3) TERTIARY: Monitor postmeal glucose curves for 1 week; if peaks persist >170 mg/dL despite carb logging + prebolus, consider split bolus (60% immediate, 40% at 120 min) or e-carb extension for specific meals. (4) OPTIONAL: Reduce max_basal from 12 to 4 U/h for safety (lower ceiling); does not address afternoon elevation but improves margin. No changes to SMB, UAM, ISF, DIA, or basal profile are needed at this time. Carb logging is the critical action item that will unlock proper control.

recommendations.title: Begin logging meal carbohydrate amounts and timing (CRITICAL PRIMARY ACTION)
recommendations.description: User must record carbohydrate grams and meal time for every meal for at least 1 week. This is the single highest-priority action because it enables AAPS to calculate proper meal boluses, prevents IOB stacking (root cause of hypoglycemic clusters), and allows SMB to micro-dose during extended GLP-1 meal absorption. Without carb logging, afternoon elevation and hypoglycemia risk cannot be resolved. This is a user-behavior change, not an automation or profile adjustment.

recommendations.title: Implement 10-minute prebolus timing after carb logging begins
recommendations.description: Once carbohydrate logging starts, deliver meal bolus (calculated by AAPS as carbs ÷ CR) approximately 10 minutes before eating or as meal begins. Rationale: insulin peaks ~90 min post-bolus (oref1 free-peak, DIA 10 h); GLP-1-delayed meal carbs peak 120–150 min post-entry; 10-min prebolus aligns insulin on-board with peak meal rise. Expected outcome: reduce postmeal glucose peaks by 10–20 mg/dL and reduce glucose variability. After 1 week, adjust to 15 min if frequent highs at 90–120 min, or 5 min if frequent lows at 60 min post-meal.

recommendations.title: Reduce max_basal from 12 U/h to 4 U/h for safety margin
recommendations.description: Current max_basal 12 U/h is 4–5× higher than oref1 guideline (2–3 U/h). Observed peak temp basal is 3.6 U/h (30% utilization), indicating ample safety margin. Reducing max_basal to 4 U/h lowers the ceiling and improves safety profile without affecting current afternoon response (which is limited by meal bolus, not basal ceiling). Implement after carb logging is established and afternoon control is improved, not urgently.

recommendations.title: Monitor postmeal glucose response for 1 week; adjust split bolus if needed
recommendations.description: After implementing carb logging + 10-min prebolus for 1 week, review postmeal glucose curves. If glucose peaks remain >170 mg/dL at 120–180 min despite correct bolus amount and prebolus timing, consider split bolus strategy (60% immediate, 40% at 120-min mark) for high-fat meals (pizza, nuts, cheese). Split bolus addresses GLP-1 absorption extended beyond 240 min. Do not implement split bolus initially; evaluate need after standard logging is working.

recommendations.title: Defer e-carb strategy until after 1 week of carb logging
recommendations.description: E-carbs (extended carbohydrate entries with duration) are not recommended initially. Standard carbohydrate logging + automatic SMB during COB window should be sufficient for typical meals. Only if persistent 3–4 hour post-meal peaks occur (despite correct bolus and prebolus timing) should e-carbs be added to specific high-fat or high-fiber meals (e.g., 20 g e-carbs over 2 h for pizza). This is a deferred optimization, not an immediate action.

recommendations.title: No changes needed to SMB, UAM, ISF, DIA, basal profile, or targets at this time
recommendations.description: Current automation configuration (SMB enabled, UAM enabled, dynamic ISF 70%, min_5m_carbimpact 8 mg/dL/5 min, etc.) is appropriate for this patient. Afternoon elevation is NOT caused by automation misconfiguration; it is caused by missing meal bolus (no carb logging). Once carbs are logged, existing SMB and UAM will function correctly without modification. Targets and basal profile are validated overnight and appropriate for GLP-1 therapy. Do not adjust these settings.

profile_recommendation.recommendation: Retain all profile settings (basal 0.5–0.8 U/h, CR 10.5–13.2 g/U, ISF 56 mg/dL/U flat, targets 90–100 mg/dL, DIA 10 h) without changes at this time. Profile is sound: overnight control (TIR 95–98%) validates basal and ISF; DIA 10 h is confirmed by correction bolus response times. CR cannot be validated without carb entries, but direction (tighter at 16:00 for afternoon resistance) is reasonable. Afternoon elevation is not a profile defect; it is caused by missing meal boluses (carb logging absent). Once user begins logging carbs, assess CR accuracy by comparing actual carbs vs. glucose response; adjust CR by ±10% only if systematic postmeal peaks or dips persist for 1 week. Do not modify basal, ISF, DIA, or targets.
profile_recommendation.rationale: Overnight glucose control is excellent (TIR 95–98%, avg 90–111 mg/dL at hours 3–7), validating basal segments and ISF 56 mg/dL/U. DIA 10 h is consistent with correction bolus responses across 24 events (typical 0.15–0.35 U boluses produce 30–50 mg/dL drops at 240 min). Afternoon elevation (hours 11–17, peak 162.8 mg/dL) occurs despite appropriate profile settings because meal carbohydrates are not being bolused (no carb entries). Basal alone (0.5–0.7 U/h) cannot contain meal carbs; basal 1.5+ U/h would be excessive and would cause overnight lows. Hypoglycemic clusters are caused by IOB stacking (high IOB from unlogged large meals + corrections), not profile error. Targets 90–100 mg/dL are appropriate for the stated age and GLP-1 therapy. CR tightens at 16:00 (10.5 g/U vs. 13 g/U at other times), appropriate for expected afternoon insulin resistance; magnitude cannot be validated without carbs. No profile change will resolve afternoon elevation or clusters without addressing meal bolus strategy first.
profile_recommendation.next_check: After user logs carbohydrate amounts for 1 week, compare actual carbs vs. observed glucose response (from therapy_response_windows) to validate CR accuracy. Calculate observed CR by dividing carb amount by glucose drop at 120 min. If observed CR differs >15% from profile (e.g., consistently lower drop than expected), adjust profile CR by 0.5–1.0 g/U. Example: if 40 g carbs consistently cause BG drop <expected at current CR, increase insulin requirement (decrease g/U denominator). After CR validation, perform similar check on afternoon ISF: if corrections during afternoon high events require >15% more insulin than profile ISF suggests, consider afternoon ISF segment (separate from flat 56). But carb logging must come first.

parameter_decisions.rationale: Hour 00 (midnight, local time 00:00–01:00 BST) shows TIR 81.5%, TBR 18.5%, avg 90.6 mg/dL. Slightly lower TIR than hours 03–07 (95–98%), suggesting basal 0.6 U/h may be marginally tight for early night. However, drop is small and not clinically concerning; no change warranted. Overnight overall (hours 00–07) achieves excellent control with this setting. Dependency: hour 00 shows early-night rebound (101.9 @ hour 01), suggesting recovery from mild drift. Hour 05–07 show basal stepping up to 0.7–0.8 U/h; current 0.6 is appropriate as transition point from sleep hours. Keep 0.6 U/h.

Hour 05 (05:00–06:00 BST, pre-dawn, pre-breakfast) shows TIR 97.5%, avg 99.5 mg/dL, TBR 2.5%. Excellent control. Basal 0.7 U/h is appropriate for dawn phenomenon transition (gradual increase from 0.6 to 0.8 U/h). Keep 0.7 U/h.

Hour 06 (06:00–07:00 BST, early morning, pre-breakfast) shows TIR 98.7%, avg 99.5 mg/dL, TBR 1.3%. Highest TIR of any hour. Basal 0.8 U/h is appropriately handling dawn phenomenon and fasting period. Keep 0.8 U/h.

Hour 10 (10:00–11:00 BST, mid-morning, post-breakfast) shows TIR 91.1%, avg 132.9 mg/dL, TAR 8.9%. Basal 0.7 U/h is same as hour 05 (pre-dawn). Elevation is modest and post-breakfast-related (meal absorption occurring). Basal is not the issue; meal bolus is. Keep 0.7 U/h. Dependency: meal carb logging required to validate whether post-breakfast elevation is unbolused carbs (no meal bolus) or carbs + late bolus.

Hour 16 (16:00–17:00 BST, afternoon, post-lunch) shows TIR 67.9%, avg 162.8 mg/dL, TAR 32.1%. This is the lowest basal in the profile (0.5 U/h) and the worst glycemic hour (peak 162.8, TAR 32.1%). Tempting to increase basal, but basal alone cannot solve this: increasing basal to 1.0 U/h (2× current) would deliver 0.5 additional U/h = 8.33 U over 14 days additional insulin, reducing afternoon dose from 275.95 to ~267.6 U/day. This modest change would be offset by meal carbs (40–50 g unbolused carbs ≈ 3–5 U per meal). Root cause is missing meal bolus, not basal insufficiency. Keep 0.5 U/h (designed to prevent afternoon lows). After meal carb logging is established and afternoon control improves, re-evaluate whether basal at 16:00 should be 0.6 U/h (matching hour 18:00) if afternoon lows become frequent. Dependency: meal carb logging must be established first; otherwise increasing basal will increase evening/overnight hypoglycemia risk without solving afternoon elevation.

Hour 18 (18:00–19:00 BST, early evening, post-dinner) shows TIR 80.4%, avg 124.2 mg/dL, TAR 11.9%. Basal 0.6 U/h is same as hour 00 (midnight). Evening is recovering from afternoon elevation toward target. Basal is appropriate. Keep 0.6 U/h.

Hour 19 (19:00–20:00 BST, evening, dinner absorption window) shows TIR 80.4%, avg 105.4 mg/dL, TBR 15.3%. Basal 0.7 U/h is designed for dinner absorption (slightly higher than hour 18:00). TBR 15.3% is elevated, but likely reflects dinner bolus effect (correction), not basal error. Keep 0.7 U/h.

CR 13 g/U at midnight (00:00) is mid-range in profile (range 10.5–13.2 g/U). Cannot validate without carb entries. Direction is reasonable (less insulin-sensitive carbs at midnight = higher denominator = less insulin per carb); consistent with night-eating being rare. Keep 13 g/U pending carb logging.

CR 11.1 g/U at 04:00 (early morning, pre-dawn, highest sensitivity = lowest denominator = most insulin per carb) reflects expected dawn phenomenon and early-morning sensitivity peak. Cannot validate without carb entries. Keep 11.1 g/U pending carb logging.

CR 13.2 g/U at 08:00 (breakfast time, decreasing sensitivity from dawn = higher denominator = less insulin per carb) is highest in profile, appropriate for breakfast being less insulin-sensitive than early morning. One meal bolus inferred (08-15 11:25, 2.4 U at BG 181, suggesting ~1.0 U meal insulin ≈ 13–15 g carbs at this CR). Consistency check possible but limited. Keep 13.2 g/U pending full carb logging.

CR 10.5 g/U at 16:00 (afternoon, lowest denominator = highest insulin per carb, reflecting expected afternoon insulin resistance) is the tightest in profile. Contradictory observation: afternoon is also the hour with worst TIR (67.9%, peak 162.8 mg/dL), suggesting underbolusing despite tight CR. Explanation: no meal carbs are being logged, so CR 10.5 g/U is not being used (no meal bolus issued). Once carbs are logged, CR 10.5 g/U can be validated. If 40 g afternoon carbs + meal bolus produces glucose drop <expected, CR may be too loose (denominator too high); tighten to 9.5–10.0 g/U. If glucose drop >expected, CR may be too tight. Keep 10.5 g/U pending carb logging and validation.
CR 12.6 g/U at 20:00 (dinner time, evening) is between breakfast 13.2 and afternoon 10.5, reflecting moderate sensitivity. Keep 12.6 g/U pending carb logging.

ISF 56 mg/dL/U (flat across 24 h) is validated by overnight correction bolus responses. Typical 0.15–0.35 U corrections produce 30–50 mg/dL drops at 240 min, consistent with ISF 56 and DIA 10 h. Overnight TIR 95–98% confirms appropriateness. Afternoon dynamic ISF drops to 37–53% (variable_sens), suggesting algorithm detects weaker sensitivity during highs; this is automatic compensation, not a profile error. ISF 56 is appropriate. Keep 56 mg/dL/U. Note: afternoon ISF weakness (variable_sens 37–53%) may indicate true afternoon insulin resistance, but more likely reflects slow meal absorption (unbolused carbs still entering at 240 min post-previous bolus, creating sustained deviation). Once carbs are logged, re-evaluate whether afternoon needs separate ISF segment (e.g., 50 mg/dL/U at 14:00–16:00). But current flat 56 is reasonable baseline.

Target 90 mg/dL at 00:00–07:59 (overnight, pre-dawn) is low (aggressive for overnight, hypoglycemia risk). However, overnight TIR 81–98% and avg 90–111 mg/dL show target is being achieved safely. Hour 00 shows TBR 18.5% (elevated), but hourly variability is normal. Hour 03–07 show TIR 95–98%, confirming target is appropriate and safely achieved. Keep 90 mg/dL overnight target.

Target 100 mg/dL at 08:00–22:59 (daytime, meal hours) is standard. Afternoon (hours 10–16) shows avg 132–163 mg/dL vs. target 100, indicating 32–63 mg/dL overshoot. This is not a target error (target is appropriate); it is caused by meal carbs not being bolused. Once carbs are logged and meal boluses are issued, afternoon glucose should fall to 110–130 mg/dL range (closer to target but still elevated due to GLP-1 slow absorption). Keep 100 mg/dL daytime target. Do not increase target to 110–120 as a band-aid; instead, focus on meal boluses.

Target 90 mg/dL at 23:00–23:59 (late evening) transitions back from daytime 100 to overnight 90. Hour 23 shows TIR 88.6%, avg 105.7 mg/dL, TBR 10.1%, indicating moderate control (slightly above target but safe). Keep 90 mg/dL late-evening target.

DIA 10 hours (insulin duration of action) is standard for oref1 free-peak model and is validated by correction bolus response times. Typical 0.15–0.35 U boluses produce expected 30–50 mg/dL drops at 240 min (60% of effect spent by 240 min in 10 h DIA). No evidence that DIA is incorrect. Keep 10 h.

Both SMB and UAM are essential and active. SMB issues micro-boluses every 3–5 min during elevated glucose (confirmed in representative_loop_statuses). UAM detects unannounced carb rises and boosts insulin (UAM Boost values 0.44–1.79 U visible). Both are functioning correctly. Afternoon elevation is not caused by SMB/UAM misconfiguration; it is upstream (meal carbs not logged). Keep both enabled.

Activation conditions are appropriate for zero-carb-entry workflow. smb_always_enabled=true allows SMB in every cycle (correct, no meal COB to wait for). smb_with_cob_enabled=false means SMB pauses during meal window (will become important once carbs are logged; ensures meal absorption before extra SMB). smb_with_temp_target_enabled=true allows SMB during temp targets (user sets temp targets sporadically; SMB appropriately allowed). smb_with_high_temp_target_enabled=false prevents SMB at very high temp targets (safety, appropriate). Keep all settings.

parameter_decisions.current_value: smb_interval_minutes=3 min; max_smb_basal_minutes=15 min; max_uam_smb_basal_minutes=20 min
parameter_decisions.rationale: smb_interval_minutes 3 min is frequent enough to detect and respond to glucose changes every 3 min. Afternoon elevation persists despite 3-min frequency, indicating constraint is downstream (meal size, absorption rate, IOB), not frequency. max_smb_basal_minutes 15 min results in max SMB ~0.125–0.175 U per dose at typical 0.5–0.7 U/h basals; conservative but safe. max_uam_smb_basal_minutes 20 min allows UAM to deliver larger SMB (0.167 U) for detected meals; appropriate. No changes needed. Keep all settings. Note: once carbs are logged, SMB will use carb-based COB rather than UAM velocity; 3-min frequency will remain sufficient.

parameter_decisions.parameter: AAPS / max basal and max IOB limits
parameter_decisions.rationale: max_basal_u_per_hour 12 U/h is 4–5× higher than oref1 guideline (2–3 U/h = 3–4× average basal 0.67 U/h). Observed peak temp basal is 3.6 U/h (30% of limit); not saturating, not constraining afternoon response. Recommend future reduction to 4 U/h for safety margin, but not urgent. Defer until after meal carb logging is established. Keep 12 U/h now. max_iob_units 25 U is appropriate and never saturates (peak observed 5.9 U = 24%). Keep 25 U. Decision: keep both now, with plan to reduce max_basal to 4 U/h after meal strategy is optimized.

autosens_enabled=false is intentional (manual tuning); no change. dynamic_sensitivity_enabled=true is active and helpful (variable_sens 37–53% during afternoon highs, indicating appropriate algorithm compensation). dynamic_isf_adjustment_factor_percent=70% is standard oref1, prevents over-correction. autosens_raises_target and autosens_lowers_target are false (no effect because autosens disabled). All settings are appropriate. Keep all.

min_5m_carbimpact 8 mg/dL/5 min is too high for GLP-1 patients with slow meal absorption (observed afternoon rise 1.5–2.2 mg/dL/5 min, below threshold). However, once user begins logging carbs, min_5m_carbimpact becomes irrelevant (explicit COB overrides UAM velocity detection). Keep 8 mg/dL/5 min now; after carbs are logged, this setting will not impact control. meal_max_absorption_hours 7 h is appropriate for GLP-1 (covers 6–8 h window with typical 7 h DIA 10 h coverage). Keep 7 h.

meal_strategy_summary.suggestion: User must begin logging meal carbohydrate amounts (grams) and timing for every meal. Once logging begins, implement 10-minute prebolus strategy: deliver AAPS-calculated meal bolus (carbs ÷ CR) approximately 10 min before eating or as meal starts. Use 100% immediate bolus (no extended/square wave); SMB will automatically micro-dose during extended GLP-1 meal absorption window if glucose rises above target. Monitor postmeal glucose curves for 1 week to validate CR accuracy and prebolus timing; adjust to 15-min prebolus if frequent highs at 90–120 min post-meal, or 5-min prebolus if frequent lows at 60 min. Do not add e-carbs initially; defer until after 1 week of logging reveals any meals with persistent 3–4 hour post-peak rises (which would trigger e-carb extension for those specific meals). Expected outcome: carb logging + meal bolus should reduce afternoon elevation by 20–30 mg/dL; 10-min prebolus should reduce peak timing and variability; correct CR validation should achieve postmeal peaks <150 mg/dL within 90–120 min; hypoglycemic clusters should resolve (carb logging prevents IOB stacking). Hypoglycemia safeguard: after first large meal bolus (>1.5 U), monitor IOB; if total IOB exceeds 5 U, defer subsequent corrections until IOB decays to <3 U (avoid stacking). All SMB, UAM, dynamic ISF, target, and basal settings should remain unchanged during this meal strategy implementation.
meal_strategy_summary.rationale: Root cause of afternoon elevation is absence of meal carbohydrate logging (zero entries over 14 days). Without carbs logged, AAPS cannot issue proactive meal boluses; all insulin is basal + corrections + SMB. Basal 0.5–0.7 U/h + SMB (max 0.125–0.175 U per dose, constrained by max_smb_basal_minutes 15) cannot contain meal carbs entering slowly (GLP-1 slows absorption to 1.5–2.2 mg/dL/5 min, below min_5m_carbimpact 8 threshold; UAM meal detection fails). Glucose rises to 160+ mg/dL before SMB catches up. Hypoglycemic clusters are caused by IOB stacking: large unlogged meal bolus (e.g., 2.4 U on 08-15) creates hidden IOB; user does not know IOB is high; subsequent correction bolus is issued; total IOB exceeds need; glucose drops >100 mg/dL (e.g., 172 → 47 mg/dL on 08-13 13:05). Carb logging enables: (1) AAPS meal bolus calculation (carbs ÷ CR), preventing unlogged-meal IOB stacking; (2) SMB respects COB window (meal_max_absorption_hours 7 h), preventing pre-meal over-correction; (3) user and algorithm transparency (both know meal amount and IOB); (4) CR validation by comparing actual carbs vs. glucose response. Prebolus timing (10 min) aligns insulin action (~90 min peak) with GLP-1 delayed meal rise (~120–150 min peak), optimizing coverage. Immediate bolus (100%) is appropriate because insulin kinetics are normal; GLP-1 slows carbs, not insulin. SMB will handle extended absorption automatically (every 3-min check, micro-dose if COB > 0 and glucose rising). E-carbs are deferred because they are a second-order optimization; standard logging + SMB should handle most meals. All automation (SMB, UAM, dynamic ISF, DIA, ISF, CR) is validated and appropriate; no changes needed. This is a user-behavior change (carb logging start) + meal timing adjustment (10-min prebolus), not an automation or profile tune.
meal_strategy_summary.next_observation: After user begins carbohydrate logging for 1 week, collect postmeal glucose response data for at least 5 meals (breakfast, lunch, dinner, each with carb amount, bolus time, and glucose curve). For each meal, calculate observed CR (carb amount ÷ glucose drop at 120 min) and compare to profile CR for that time segment. If observed CR differs >15% from profile, adjust profile CR by 0.5–1.0 g/U (e.g., if 40 g carbs cause smaller drop than expected, patient is more insulin-resistant; decrease CR g/U to increase insulin delivery). Also observe whether postmeal peak occurs at 60, 90, or 120 min; if consistently at 90 min or later, prebolus timing is appropriate; if at 60 min or earlier, consider reducing prebolus to 5 min. This 1-week validation is critical before any profile adjustments.

exceptions.pattern: Hypoglycemic cluster risk (IOB stacking): Occurs when large unlogged meal bolus (e.g., 2+ U) is followed by correction bolus without accounting for meal IOB.
exceptions.observed_pattern: 08-13 17:00–17:14 (4 lows 42–51 mg/dL) preceded by iob 1.628 U + 0.2 U bolus; 08-14 18:00–18:14 (3 lows 41–48 mg/dL) with similar pattern.
exceptions.suggestion: With carb logging implemented, AAPS will track meal IOB transparently; algorithm will not issue corrections if COB > 0 (meal still absorbing). User safeguard: after issuing bolus >1.5 U, wait 2 hours before issuing next bolus; allow IOB to decay to <2 U. Monitor glucose during 60–180 min post-bolus; if drops below 80 mg/dL, bolus was too large (meal was smaller than estimated); reduce next meal's bolus by 0.3 U. Expect complete elimination of cluster pattern once carbs are logged.
exceptions.rationale: Root cause: IOB stacking from unlogged meals. With carbs logged, algorithm knows meal IOB; prevents over-correction. User discipline (wait 2 h between large boluses) adds safety margin. This exception resolves automatically once carb logging starts; no configuration change needed.

exceptions.pattern: Afternoon elevation despite prebolus (hours 14–16): Persistent BG >170 mg/dL at 120–180 min post-meal despite correct carb amount, prebolus timing, and CR.
exceptions.observed_pattern: 08-15 11:25 bolus (2.4 U, 181 mg/dL start) produces rebound rise by 180–240 min (94 @ 120m, 130 @ 180m, 188 @ 240m), suggesting continued meal carb absorption beyond 240 min.
exceptions.suggestion: If postmeal peaks >170 mg/dL persist (1) increase prebolus to 15 min (extends insulin on-board into later absorption phase); (2) verify SMB is issuing micro-boluses during meal window (check app logs for SMB doses every 3–5 min at 60–180 min post-meal); (3) if peaks persist despite SMB, consider split bolus for that meal (60% immediate, 40% at 120-min mark) or e-carb extension (20 g e-carbs over 2 h for high-fat meals like pizza). Do not implement split bolus initially; evaluate need after 1 week standard logging shows persistent pattern.
exceptions.rationale: GLP-1 extends meal absorption to 240+ min; upfront bolus may be mostly exhausted by 180 min when carbs are still entering. Split bolus or e-carb extends insulin action into later absorption phase. This is a deferred optimization (only if standard strategy fails); most meals should be manageable with standard logging + 10-min prebolus + SMB.

implementation_steps.title: Begin carbohydrate logging immediately
implementation_steps.description: Starting with the next meal, user should log carbohydrate amount (in grams) and meal time in AAPS for every meal. Include meal type if possible (simple carbs, complex, high-fat, etc.). Do not estimate; use food labels, smartphone app (MyFitnessPal, etc.), or ask dietitian for portion sizes. Log for minimum 1 week (14+ meals). This is the critical action that enables all downstream improvements.

implementation_steps.title: Wait until 5+ meals are logged before implementing prebolus timing
implementation_steps.description: Do not change bolus timing until AAPS has sufficient data to learn patient's pattern. AAPS will calculate meal boluses automatically (carbs ÷ CR) once carbs are entered. Observe first 5 meals (can span 1–2 days) to confirm AAPS calculations are working in the app. If AAPS shows 'calculated bolus' but does not match user expectation (e.g., expected 3 U but AAPS calculates 1.5 U), verify CR setting is correct (should be tightest at lunch/afternoon hours).

implementation_steps.title: Implement 10-minute prebolus for breakfast and lunch (days 2–3 of logging)
implementation_steps.description: Once carbs are logged and AAPS calculates meal bolus, deliver bolus approximately 10 min before eating or as meal starts. Start with breakfast and lunch (daytime meals); dinner can follow once confidence is high. Prebolus timing: set phone alarm 10 min before planned meal; at alarm, open AAPS, enter carbs, confirm bolus, and approve delivery. Eat meal 10 min after bolus is delivered. Record bolus time in notes for reference (e.g., 'bolus 1.5 U at 12:30, ate at 12:40').

implementation_steps.title: Monitor postmeal glucose curves for 1 week; adjust prebolus timing if needed
implementation_steps.description: After 5+ meals with prebolus, observe postmeal glucose peaks: are peaks occurring at 60, 90, 120, or 150+ min post-meal? Target peak timing is 90–120 min post-meal start (or 80–110 min post-bolus if prebolus is 10 min early). If peaks occur at 60 min (too early), patient may be more insulin-sensitive than expected; try reducing prebolus to 5 min. If peaks occur at 120+ min (too late), or if peaks >170 mg/dL persist, increase prebolus to 15 min. Adjust one prebolus time per week; do not change multiple variables simultaneously.

implementation_steps.title: After 1 week of carb logging, validate carbohydrate ratio (CR) accuracy
implementation_steps.description: Review 1 week of meals. For each meal, record: (1) carb amount (from log), (2) glucose at bolus time (from CGM), (3) glucose at 120 min post-meal (from CGM), (4) bolus amount (from AAPS log). Calculate observed glucose drop: glucose_120m − glucose_bolus. Calculate expected drop: (carbs ÷ CR) × ISF 56. Compare observed vs. expected. If observed drop is 15%+ smaller than expected, patient may need tighter CR (smaller g/U denominator) for that meal time. If observed drop is 15%+ larger than expected, CR may be too tight. Adjust CR by ±0.5–1.0 g/U and re-test for 1 week. Example: if 40 g lunch carbs (CR 10.5 g/U = 3.8 U bolus) but glucose drops only 20 mg/dL (instead of expected 50 mg/dL from 3.8 U × ISF 56), carbs may be underestimated or CR too loose; try CR 9.5 g/U (4.2 U for same 40 g) and observe.

implementation_steps.title: Monitor for hypoglycemia during first week of meal boluses; adjust if clusters recur
implementation_steps.description: Hypoglycemic clusters (08-13, 08-14) are expected to resolve once carbs are logged (IOB stacking eliminated). If lows (<70 mg/dL) occur despite carb logging, check whether bolus was too large (meal was smaller than user estimated). If glucose drops >80 mg/dL in first 2 hours post-bolus, reduce next bolus by 0.3 U. If lows persist, also check whether basal is too high (overnight lows suggest 0.6 U/h at 00:00 is too much; reduce to 0.5 U/h and re-test). But do not make changes to basal until carb logging is stable (1+ week).

implementation_steps.title: After 1 week carb logging, decide on e-carb strategy
implementation_steps.description: Review 1 week of postmeal glucose curves. Identify any meals that produced peaks >170 mg/dL at 120–180 min post-meal despite correct bolus and prebolus timing. These meals are candidates for e-carb extension. For high-fat or high-fiber meals (pizza, nuts, fried foods, salads), try adding e-carbs: log same carbs as before, then add 20–30 g e-carbs with 2-hour duration. Re-test that meal 1–2 times. If peak drops to <150 mg/dL, e-carbs are helping; retain them. If no change, remove e-carbs (e.g., split bolus may be more effective for that meal). Do not add e-carbs to all meals; only those with demonstrated persistent peaks.

implementation_steps.title: Do not make automation or basal changes during the first 2 weeks of carb logging
implementation_steps.description: Carb logging is the single highest-priority change. While implementing carb logging, do not simultaneously adjust SMB, UAM, max basal, max IOB, targets, or basal profile. These settings are validated and appropriate. Changing multiple variables will make it impossible to isolate the effect of carb logging. After 2 weeks of stable carb logging and improved afternoon control, consider secondary optimizations (e.g., reduce max_basal to 4 U/h, adjust CR, add e-carbs). Safety: if glucose control worsens during carb logging (e.g., frequent highs >200 or frequent lows <70), contact care team before adjusting settings.

implementation_steps.title: Optional: Reduce max_basal from 12 U/h to 4 U/h after meal strategy is optimized (week 3+)
implementation_steps.description: After 2+ weeks of stable carb logging and improved afternoon control, consider reducing max_basal from 12 U/h to 4 U/h for safety margin. This lowers the ceiling without affecting current control (observed peak temp basal is only 3.6 U/h). Implement by changing one setting in AAPS, testing for 2–3 days, and confirming no unexpected high BG or reduced temp basal response. Defer this change until after carb logging is stable and afternoon elevation is resolved.

education.content: Carbohydrate logging enables AAPS to calculate appropriate meal insulin doses. Without logging, AAPS assumes zero carbs (COB = 0) and relies only on SMB/UAM to detect rises and issue corrections. This is reactive (waiting for glucose to rise) rather than proactive (preventing the rise). GLP-1 therapy slows meal carb absorption; even with SMB every 3 minutes, basal + SMB cannot match the rate of slow carb entry. Result: glucose rises to 160+ mg/dL before being controlled. Carb logging solves this by enabling AAPS to issue a meal bolus upfront, with SMB topping up if absorption is slow. Expected outcome: afternoon peaks drop from 160+ to 130–150 mg/dL; time-in-range improves from 86% to 90%+.

education.topic: How prebolus timing works with GLP-1
education.content: Insulin peaks ~90 min after injection (oref1 free-peak model, DIA 10 h). Carbs start raising glucose immediately upon absorption but peak 60–120 min after eating (normal absorption). GLP-1 delays both: carb entry is slower (1.5–2 mg/dL/5 min instead of 3–5 mg/dL/5 min), and peak is delayed to 120–150 min. Prebolus (giving insulin 10 min before eating) shifts insulin peak from 90 min post-bolus to ~100 min post-carb-entry. This aligns insulin action with GLP-1-delayed meal rise. Example: eat at 12:30 pm; bolus at 12:20 pm; insulin peaks at 1:50 pm; meal carbs peak at 1:50–2:10 pm; excellent overlap = glucose controlled. Without prebolus (bolus at 12:30), insulin peaks at 2:00 pm; meal carbs still rising at 2:00 pm; overshoot occurs before insulin is fully effective.

education.topic: How IOB stacking causes hypoglycemic clusters
education.content: IOB (insulin on board) is the total insulin active in bloodstream from all sources (basal, boluses, SMB). With 10-hour DIA, insulin from a meal bolus given at noon is still 50% active at 5 pm. If user gives another bolus at 2 pm (for lunch or correction), total IOB at 2 pm = noon bolus IOB + 2 pm bolus IOB. If both boluses were large and unlogged, user does not know IOB is high. A small correction at 5 pm (0.2 U) + hidden high IOB can cause excessive drop (125 mg/dL, as observed 08-13). Carb logging makes IOB visible: AAPS shows 'meal IOB 1.5 U' so user knows not to add more insulin until IOB decays. This prevents cluster risk.

education.topic: Why all other settings are appropriate (no automation or profile changes needed now)
education.content: Overnight control is excellent (TIR 95–98%), validating basal and ISF. DIA 10 h is confirmed by correction bolus responses. SMB every 3 min, UAM, dynamic ISF, and safety limits are all functioning correctly (active, not saturating). Afternoon elevation appears to be an automation/profile problem but is actually a meal strategy problem: meal carbs are not being bolused. Once carbs are logged and meal boluses are issued, SMB and existing settings will work correctly without modification. Changing settings before carb logging is in place will make it impossible to isolate the effect of carb logging and may introduce new problems. Trust the existing configuration; focus on carb logging.

GLP-1 (semaglutide, tirzepatide) slows gastric emptying (stomach-to-intestine), delaying carbohydrate absorption by 30–60% compared to non-GLP-1 baseline. This is intentional (GLP-1 improves glucose control by reducing post-meal spikes). However, insulin absorption is NOT delayed by GLP-1; insulin is absorbed normally from subcutaneous injection. This means a single upfront meal bolus (100% immediate) combined with SMB (micro-dosing throughout absorption) is the correct strategy, not extended bolus (slow insulin release), which would mismatch normal insulin kinetics. DIA 10 h is long enough to cover a 240+ min meal; no need for extended bolus as long as carbs are logged (AAPS knows how long absorption will last and can SMB throughout).

education.topic: Glucose targets and 'acceptable' control on GLP-1
education.content: Targets 90–100 mg/dL daytime are standard for type 1 diabetes. GLP-1 improves long-term glucose control and reduces hypoglycemia risk, allowing these targets to be safely pursued. Current afternoon average 162.8 mg/dL at hour 16 is above target but not dangerous; overnight TIR 95–98% shows control is possible. Once meal carbs are logged and meal boluses are optimized, afternoon glucose should fall to 130–150 mg/dL range (closer to target, though slightly elevated due to slow GLP-1 absorption and afternoon insulin resistance). Do not increase targets to 110–120 in afternoon as a shortcut; instead, optimize meal boluses first. Some afternoon elevation is expected and acceptable on GLP-1; the goal is to prevent >150 mg/dL sustained peaks.

safety_notes: This is decision-support analysis only. All proposed changes must be reviewed and approved by the user's care team (endocrinologist, diabetes educator) before implementation. Do not change AAPS settings automatically; user must understand and approve each change.

Carbohydrate logging is a user-behavior change, not an automation change. User must be able to estimate meal carbohydrate amounts accurately. Recommend using a food scale, smartphone app (MyFitnessPal), or consulting a registered dietitian for portion/carb training.

Prebolus timing (10 min before eating) requires discipline and planning. User must eat within 10–15 min of bolus; delayed eating increases hypoglycemia risk (insulin active, carbs not yet entering). User should confirm access to food before giving bolus.

Hypoglycemia safeguard: if glucose drops below 70 mg/dL (hypoglycemia), follow standard sick-day rules (treat with fast carbs, retest in 15 min, contact care team if persistent). Do not drive or operate machinery during hypoglycemia. Hypoglycemic clusters on 08-13 and 08-14 are expected to resolve once carbs are logged; if they recur after logging starts, contact care team immediately.

Do not make multiple changes simultaneously. Change carb logging strategy first (2 weeks), then add prebolus (1 week), then optimize CR (1 week), then consider e-carbs or basal adjustments. This sequential approach isolates the effect of each change.

Monitor glucose continuously using CGM during implementation. If TIR drops or time-below-range increases after carb logging starts, contact care team; medication adjustments may be needed. Expected outcome is improvement (TIR increase, TAR decrease) within 1 week of carb logging; if not improving, troubleshoot with care team.

Afternoon target 100 mg/dL may not be achievable on GLP-1 with perfect meal boluses. Acceptable afternoon glucose range on GLP-1 is 110–150 mg/dL (vs. target 90–100). Do not over-correct during afternoon if peaks are 140–150 mg/dL and COB > 0 (meal still absorbing); wait for absorption to complete before correcting. Over-correction causes the hypoglycemic clusters observed on 08-13, 08-14.

GLP-1 therapy side effects (nausea, gastroparesis, reduced appetite) may affect meal size and carbohydrate estimation. If GLP-1 side effects are present, user may accidentally under-estimate carbs (feeling full, eating less than anticipated portion). Monitor postmeal glucose; if trends show persistent underestimation (peaks >170 mg/dL despite adequate bolus), increase carb estimates or CR tightness.

Device changes (site changes, sensor changes, profile switches) were documented on multiple dates (08-10, 08-11, 08-13, 08-17, 08-21). Device changes can affect insulin absorption and sensor accuracy. After a device change, glucose control may be transiently disrupted; allow 2–3 h for absorption site to stabilize before interpreting control. Do not make AAPS changes within 2 h of infusion set or sensor change.

If user is pregnant, planning pregnancy, or has other major life changes (travel, illness, surgery), consult care team before implementing this analysis. Pregnancy requires tighter glucose targets and may necessitate different carb estimation strategies.
This analysis is based on 14 days of data (2026-08-07 to 2026-08-21). If more than 1 month passes without re-analysis, request updated analysis; AAPS settings or GLP-1 dose may have changed.

User must have access to AAPS app on their phone with working CGM (Dexcom, Freestyle Libre, etc.) and compatible insulin pump. Carbohydrate logging is entered into AAPS via the app; if app crashes or CGM loses signal, glucose control may be temporarily disrupted.
